title: Grounded and Well-Designed Responses · Level 2
slo: Choose prompt and retrieval practices that produce a more relevant response.

exercises.question_text: Providing an example can help a model reproduce a requested style.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Without a concrete style guide, the reply may not match the approved tone a writer needs.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Provide an example when you want a particular style and need to show what that style looks like.

exercises.explanation: Correct—an example makes the desired style concrete. It helps guide the wording and tone of the response.

exercises.question_text: A response is grounded when it is based only on the conversation history.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Relying only on earlier messages may leave out the facts needed for the current question.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Earlier conversation can be useful context. A grounded response is based on relevant information supplied in the prompt.

exercises.explanation: Correct—conversation history can add context, but it is not the definition of grounding. Grounding uses relevant information supplied in the prompt.

exercises.question_text: Prompts with explicit instructions are more ___ than vague prompts.

parts.text: Prompts with explicit instructions are more

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A vague request can lead to a response that does not match the intended task.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: The missing phrase is clear and specific. Examples show style, and response structure organizes a reply, but explicit instructions make the prompt itself clear.

exercises.explanation: Explicit instructions make the requested task easier to understand than vague language. Examples and response structure can help too, but they are particular additions rather than the overall quality named here.

exercises.question_text: Put the pieces in the correct order.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The purpose of the sample becomes unclear when its connection to the desired style is broken.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Keep the logic together: provide a sample when the desired style needs to be made concrete.

exercises.correct_answer: Provide an example when the desired style needs to be made concrete
exercises.explanation: A style can be hard to describe with general words alone. Providing a concrete sample helps show the style the response should reproduce.

exercises.question_text: A communications employee must ask an assistant for a summary of generative AI adoption for corporate executives. Which prompt should the employee send?

options.text: Summarize AI adoption for executives in six bullets
options.rationale: This request identifies the topic, audience, and desired format. It gives explicit instructions for the needed summary.
The task and topic are present, but the audience is missing. The requested format is also not stated.
options.better_fit: This fits a situation where any audience and format are acceptable. Add more context for a corporate-executive summary.

feedback.intrinsic: The employee may receive a summary that is not suited to executives or is hard to scan.
feedback.instructional: Add the intended audience and format when they matter. Here, executives and six bullets make the request more useful.

options.rationale: A writing sample can guide style. This instruction does not ask for a summary or identify the topic and audience.
options.better_fit: This fits style guidance alongside a complete request. Use it when a desired style needs to be shown.

feedback.intrinsic: The response may imitate a style but fail to summarize generative AI adoption for executives.
feedback.instructional: A complete prompt says what to do and for whom. Add a sample only when style guidance is also needed.

options.error_type: Confuses complete prompt with structure alone
options.rationale: This requests an organization but gives no topic or audience. It is only one part of a clear and specific prompt.
options.better_fit: This fits a format instruction added to a full request. Use it when the content and audience have already been stated.

feedback.intrinsic: The response may be numbered but not address the executive summary task.
feedback.instructional: A structure request helps organize a response; it does not replace the topic, task, and audience.

exercises.explanation: Correct—it clearly names the topic, audience, and format. That gives the assistant a focused request to follow.

exercises.question_text: A customer-support writer needs an assistant to create replies in the same style as an approved customer reply. Which actions should the writer take? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: The approved reply provides a concrete model of the desired style. Including it gives the writer's style request something specific to follow.

options.text: Ask the model to follow its style
options.rationale: This instruction explains how the approved reply should be used. It connects the sample to the new replies being requested.
Expense-policy sections provide factual context for expense questions. They do not demonstrate the style of an approved customer reply.
options.better_fit: This fits a reply that must answer an expense-policy question. Use it when relevant policy facts are needed.

feedback.intrinsic: The new reply may include unrelated expense details and still fail to match the approved customer style.
feedback.instructional: For style matching, provide the approved reply and ask to follow its style. Retrieve policy sections only when policy facts are needed.

options.rationale: Earlier messages can maintain conversational context. They do not necessarily show the approved style the writer wants to reproduce.
options.better_fit: This fits retaining context from an ongoing exchange. It is useful when a follow-up depends on what was previously said.

feedback.intrinsic: The reply may continue the conversation but not match the approved customer-reply style.
feedback.instructional: Conversation history preserves context. A selected approved reply is the concrete style example needed here.

exercises.explanation: Correct—include the approved reply and explicitly ask to follow its style. Together, those actions make the desired style concrete.

exercises.question_text: The approach that retrieves relevant documents and adds them to a prompt is ___.

parts.text: The approach that retrieves relevant documents and adds them to a prompt is

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The prompt would not name the approach used to bring relevant documents into the answer.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Use retrieval augmented generation, or RAG. Do not confuse it with conversation history or with the grounded response that relevant information can support.

exercises.explanation: The term names a process that first retrieves relevant information and then augments the prompt with it. Conversation history uses earlier messages, while a grounded response is the result of using relevant supplied information.

exercises.question_text: Reconstruct the statement from the pieces.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The relationship between supplied information and response relevance becomes unclear.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Connect the cause to the outcome: relevant prompt information can make a response more relevant.

exercises.correct_answer: Relevant prompt information can make a response more relevant
exercises.explanation: Relevant information supplied with a request gives a response a factual basis and can make it more relevant. This differs from merely preserving earlier conversation context.

exercises.question_text: An employee asks an expenses assistant for the maximum travel claim. Before the assistant answers, what should its developer have the app do?

options.rationale: The relevant policy sections contain the organization-specific information needed for the question. They can be added to the prompt before a response is generated.

options.text: Use only the employee's last message
options.rationale: The employee's question identifies the topic but does not provide the maximum claim amount. Relevant policy information is still needed.
options.better_fit: This fits using the latest request as part of conversation context. It is not enough when the answer depends on company policy.

feedback.intrinsic: The employee may receive a generic answer instead of the company rule.
feedback.instructional: The question tells what to look for. Retrieve the relevant travel-policy sections to provide the facts.

options.rationale: A numbered list can make a response easier to read. It does not provide the travel-expense rule.
options.better_fit: This fits a request to organize an answer. It can be added after the relevant policy is supplied.

feedback.intrinsic: The employee may get a tidy list without learning the correct claim limit.
feedback.instructional: Format and factual grounding solve different needs. Retrieve the policy when the question depends on policy facts.

options.error_type: Confuses retrieval with examples in prompts
options.rationale: A style sample can show how a reply should sound. It does not supply the travel-expense policy.
options.better_fit: This fits a request to match a desired writing style. Use it when tone or style needs to be made concrete.

feedback.intrinsic: The answer could sound polished while still missing the correct company rule.
feedback.instructional: A style example guides wording. Relevant retrieved policy information supplies the facts for this question.

exercises.explanation: Correct—retrieving the relevant travel-expense policy is the RAG step. It gives the prompt information that can ground the answer.

exercises.question_text: A request for bullet points or a table specifies the response ___.

parts.text: A request for bullet points or a table specifies the response

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The requested reply could be organized in the wrong way because the organization term is missing.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: The missing term is structure. Examples in prompts guide style, while clear and specific prompts describe the quality of the overall request.

exercises.explanation: Bullet points and tables determine how a response is organized. They do not themselves show a writing style or describe the overall clarity of the prompt.

exercises.question_text: A manager asks an expenses assistant about travel claims. The assistant must answer using the company rules. Which actions help make its answer grounded? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Relevant travel-policy sections provide the company rules for the answer. Supplying them in the prompt grounds the response.
The manager's question identifies what information the response should address. Combined with relevant policy sections, it helps focus the grounded answer.

options.text: Use a generic answer without policy text
options.rationale: A generic answer is not based on the company's supplied travel rules. It may not answer the manager's policy question with relevant information.
options.better_fit: This fits a situation with no organization-specific information available. It is weaker when company rules are required.

feedback.intrinsic: The manager may receive advice that does not match the company's travel rules.
feedback.instructional: For a grounded policy answer, include relevant policy information with the manager's question.

options.rationale: A table tells how to organize information. It does not provide the company rules on which an answer must be based.
options.better_fit: This fits a need to compare or organize information in a table. It can be used together with relevant supplied policy sections.

feedback.intrinsic: The manager may get a clear table that still lacks the company rule.
feedback.instructional: Structure can improve readability, but grounding requires relevant information in the prompt.

exercises.explanation: Correct—include the question and the relevant travel-policy sections. The policy sections provide the facts that ground the response.

exercises.question_text: A manager asks an assistant to prepare project risks for a meeting. The manager needs the risks presented clearly. Which instruction should be added?

options.text: Present the risks in a table
options.rationale: A table specifies how the project risks should be organized. It can help present the risks clearly for the meeting.
A friendly sample reply guides tone or style. It does not specify how to organize project risks.
options.better_fit: This fits a situation where a friendly writing style is needed. It is useful when the desired tone needs a concrete sample.

feedback.intrinsic: The manager may receive a friendly-sounding response that is still difficult to scan in the meeting.
feedback.instructional: Use a table when the need is clear organization. Use a sample reply when the need is to demonstrate tone or style.

options.rationale: Travel-policy sections provide information for travel-expense questions. They do not organize project risks for a meeting.
options.better_fit: This fits a travel-expense question that needs relevant company policy information. It does not address this formatting need.

feedback.intrinsic: The meeting material could include unrelated travel information and still present risks poorly.
feedback.instructional: Retrieved information adds facts. A table is the instruction that directly controls how the project risks are presented.

options.rationale: The project-risk topic is already part of the request. This instruction does not say how the risks should be organized.
options.better_fit: This fits adding topic context to an incomplete request. It is unnecessary when the topic is already clear.

feedback.intrinsic: The manager may still get an unstructured list that is difficult to use during the meeting.
feedback.instructional: The missing need is organization. Add a format instruction such as presenting the risks in a table.

exercises.explanation: Correct—a table is a clear response-structure request. It tells how to present the project risks for easier scanning.
